executive_summary: AUD/JPY trades at 110.92, having fallen 3.85% from the 114.46 close of 27 July in five consecutive weekday declines — the pair's worst five-session run in fifteen months — after the United States and Japan executed their first coordinated yen-buying intervention in nearly three decades on Friday 31 July. The pair is down 2.00% over one month and 3.04% over three months, but still up 0.91% over six months and 10.14% over twelve, sitting at the 82nd percentile of a 52-week range spanning 92.31 to 114.92. The dominant bilateral narrative has changed in the space of four sessions: what was a 335bp carry engine grinding toward multi-decade highs is now a crowded carry trade being actively dismantled by an official-sector coalition, with the US Treasury confirming it 'countered disorderly yen movements,' stating it 'will not hesitate to participate in further joint intervention,' and endorsing Japan's steps 'to correct the substantial undervaluation of the yen.' Three bilateral differentials diverge sharply from what the standalone dossiers imply: first, the AUD dossier's tactically bullish AUD view rests on a 4.35% policy rate that is at a plateau, while the JPY dossier's bullish yen view rests on a policy rate 100bp below the BoJ's own stated neutral — so the +335bp differential can only narrow from here, not widen; second, the pair-implied positioning extreme is almost entirely a funding-leg phenomenon (a combined 185,047-contract yen net short against a merely mid-range 24,788-contract AUD long), meaning the unwind fuel is roughly eight times more concentrated on the leg that has just been attacked; third, the real-exchange-rate gap is the widest in the G10, with Australia's REER at 115.92 (97th percentile, +9.8% y/y) against Japan's at 65.30 (an all-time low, -11.8% y/y), a 21.6 percentage point twelve-month divergence that puts relative-REER fair value near 96 against spot at 110.92. Offsetting this is the one genuinely bullish bilateral: the terms-of-trade channel, where Australia's $29.0bn goods surplus with Japan consists overwhelmingly of the LNG, coal and iron ore whose prices have surged, mechanically transferring income from Tokyo to Canberra. We are tactically Bearish the pair with conviction 4 (weighted score -0.3713), targeting 108.50 over two to four weeks, and strategically Bearish with conviction 3 (weighted score -0.3481), targeting 104.00 — with the explicit caveat that a short pays away 31 pips of carry every month and that this exact thesis has cost money for twelve consecutive months.

market_context.valuation_assessment: Both dossiers independently place the pair 14-15% rich on a relative-REER basis: the AUD dossier's PPP table gives an implied AUD/JPY fair value of 96.60 (+15.44% deviation), and the JPY dossier's mirror calculation gives 95.68 (yen 14.2% cheap to AUD, the widest gap in the entire G10-plus-SGD matrix). Against spot at 110.92 that is 14.7% to 15.9% of overvaluation. Australia's BIS real broad effective rate printed 115.92 in June 2026, 6.4% above its 30-month mean and at the 97th percentile after a 9.8% real appreciation, while Japan's printed 65.30, 7.8% below its own mean after an 11.8% real depreciation and the lowest reading ever recorded on that series — a 21.6 percentage point twelve-month real divergence. Nominally the pair sits close to multi-decade extremes, having hit its highest level since the early 1990s in March 2026 and made a marginal new high at 114.92 on 2 June. What the current level prices is a permanent 335bp carry differential, a permanent Japanese energy-import penalty, and no official-sector reaction function on the yen side — the third of those propositions was falsified on 31 July.

market_context.recent_regime: The regime through 27 July was the purest expression of the global carry trade available: a 335bp differential, realised volatility near 4.5%, VIX at 17.09, US high-yield spreads at 281-287bp within touching distance of generational tights, and a pair grinding within 50 pips of a multi-decade high. That regime ended in four sessions via a rare coordinated yen-buying intervention to halt the currency's slide to 40-year lows, the first joint action since 2011. The dominant narrative for the next month is whether official action plus a hawkish BoJ can convert a positioning squeeze into a trend.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The RBA cash rate of 4.35% against the BoJ's around 1.0 percent target gives an annualised policy-rate carry of +335bp, the widest carry differential in the G10. Against 20-day realised volatility of 9.1% the carry-to-vol ratio is 0.37; against the 60-day realised figure of 7.21% it is 0.46; against estimated 3M implied of roughly 10% it is 0.34 — a material deterioration from the 0.46 published pre-event, entirely through the denominator. Carry has stopped working for this pair: the conditions under which 335bp dominates are low realised volatility and an absent official reaction function on the funding leg, and both have reversed. The 441-pip decline from 114.46 to 110.05 erased approximately 14.2 months of accrued carry in four trading sessions.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The differential is +335bp on policy rates, +307bp on the two-year (ACGB 4.57% against JGB 1.497%) and +213bp on the ten-year (ACGB 4.93% against JGB 2.801%), and every one of those gaps is narrower than it was twelve months ago even as the pair rose 10.14%. The trajectory is unambiguously one-directional: the RBA is at a plateau with the 29 July CPI undershoot at 3.8% headline cutting 11 August hike odds from above 90% to roughly a coin flip, while the BoJ sits 100bp below its own board's stated neutral of 'around 2 percent' with only 21bp of cumulative tightening priced through 18 December. The pricing question is where the surprise distribution lies, and it is asymmetric against the pair: an RBA hike on 11 August is roughly half-priced and would widen the gap to 360bp, whereas Japanese September pricing at 16-35% sits against a governor who has said the Bank could speed up the pace of hikes and a board member already voting for 1.25%. The transmission to this specific pair is more direct than to any other cross, because AUD/JPY is the pair in which the entire differential is expressed as carry rather than as a growth or terms-of-trade story. Note also the real-rate differential, which is where the asymmetry is starkest: Australia runs a policy rate 55bp above its own headline inflation while Japan runs one 70bp below, so Japan has 125bp of real-rate normalisation available before it even matches Australia's stance. Inside the tactical window the dated tests are the 10 August BoJ Summary of Opinions and the 11 August RBA decision, back-to-back, in that order.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the differential can only narrow, and the question is by how much and through which leg. The base path — one BoJ hike to 1.25% and an RBA hold — takes the gap from 335bp to 310bp. The path implied by the BoJ's own framework of 25bp steps toward 2% neutral, combined with CBA's expectation of Australian cuts in 2027, takes it toward 210-235bp inside twelve months, the narrowest AU-JP differential since 2022. A 100bp compression is 30% of the entire economic rationale for holding AUD/JPY, and the pair has no other rationale of comparable weight. Against that, the strategically honest counter is the disconfirming evidence embedded in the last twelve months: the ten-year JGB rose roughly 122bp year-on-year, compressing the AU-JP ten-year spread meaningfully, and AUD/JPY rose 10.14% anyway, because the rise in Japanese yields was a fiscal risk premium concentrated in the super-long end rather than a policy premium in the front end. The observable test that distinguishes the two regimes is which part of the JGB curve leads the next move: front-end-led confirms the rate channel and is bearish the pair, super-long-led confirms the fiscal channel and is bullish it. The pair's own history says do not assume the former.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The inflation differential is +210bp on headline (Australia 3.8% against Japan 1.7%) and +200bp on preferred core measures, which looks decisively pair-bullish until you look at the direction of travel, which is convergent from both ends simultaneously. Australia's headline path over five months runs 4.6% to 3.8% and the trimmed mean has been flat at 3.6% for two months; Japan's Tokyo July print, released 31 July, came in at 2.0% headline, 1.9% core against a 1.7% consensus, all accelerating. Tokyo leads the national series by roughly a month, so the 20 August national release is the highest-impact single data event in the tactical window, and it is a Japanese release. The asymmetric-sensitivity conclusion cuts against the standalone dossiers: because the RBA's reaction function is already saturated while the BoJ's is 100bp from neutral with almost nothing priced, a given basis point of Japanese inflation surprise moves this pair considerably more than the same surprise in Australia. On growth the differential still favours the base — Australia 2.5% year-on-year against Japan 0.32% — but the momentum differential has inverted: Japan's June Tankan showed large manufacturers at +22 and non-manufacturers at +37 (highest since August 1991) with a July composite PMI at a five-month high of 53.1, while Australian consumer sentiment at 83.9 and NAB business confidence at -5 both sit in the bottom decile.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the relevant differential is not the level of inflation but the credibility of each economy's inflation-expectations regime, because that determines relative terminal rates. Japan's evidence is now unusually strong: corporate expectations at 2.7%, 2.6% and 2.6% across one-, three- and five-year horizons all above target, a household survey showing 90.4% expecting price rises (a series record since 2006), a third consecutive shunto above 5%, and nominal earnings above 3% for four consecutive months, the longest run since 1992. Australia's evidence points the other way: WPI of 3.3% below headline inflation, real wages down 0.8%, quarterly wage growth pinned at 0.8% since September 2025. In relative terms, the economy with the higher measured inflation has the weaker expectations mechanism and the economy with the lower measured inflation has the stronger one — precisely backwards from what the +200bp core differential suggests. Growth-cycle positioning reinforces it: Australia is late-cycle with 75bp of 2026 tightening still transmitting into a 0.3% quarterly GDP print, while Japan is early-cycle with a slightly positive output gap and the strongest Tankan readings in three decades.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Every observable risk gauge is currently supportive of the pair and yet the pair has fallen 3.85% in five sessions, which is the whole analytical content of this factor. VIX closed at 17.09, US IG spreads near 80bp, HY at 281-287bp within roughly 46bp of a generational low, S&P 500 finished July near 7,490 at a record, and copper is up roughly 46% year-on-year near a 2026 record — the exact configuration in which the highest-beta risk cross in G10 outperforms. It did not, because the transmission channel that moved the pair was positioning and official flow, not risk aversion: the yen rallied 3.4% in two sessions on a day the VIX did not spike. That is diagnostically important, because the pair is currently vulnerable to a channel entirely independent of the risk gauges everyone monitors. The bilateral beta differential remains extreme — AUD is the highest-beta G10 currency to global risk and AUD/JPY is the purest risk barometer in G10 FX — so if the risk tape does crack, this is the pair that moves furthest. The offsetting observation is that the equity and credit backdrop is genuinely benign with no dated catalyst inside four weeks that reliably breaks it. One crack worth naming is that the Nikkei fell as much as 2.5% as the stronger currency weighed on exporters, the reflexive channel through which yen strength itself becomes a risk-negative event.

The one honest offset is that the yen's safe-haven property has been genuinely degraded by the energy channel: USD/JPY has been showing positive relationships with bond and equity volatility while remaining negatively correlated with equities, behaving more like a risk asset than a haven.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the highest-confidence factor in the analysis, and its bilateral content is genuinely different from either standalone view. Netting the two legs, speculative money is long the base and short the quote — leveraged funds +24,788 AUD contracts against -101,990 JPY contracts — so the pair signal is amplified rather than muted. But the amplification is lopsided: the AUD long is roughly USD 1.74bn notional at approximately the 50th percentile of its trailing year and less than a third of the ±80,000-contract level at which AUD reversals historically become actionable, while the combined JPY net short is 185,047 contracts, roughly USD 14.6bn, beyond the -150,000 threshold. The crowding is approximately eight-to-one a funding-leg phenomenon, meaning the pair does not require Australian long liquidation to fall — it requires only yen short covering, and the yen short was still growing by 8,956 contracts in the week to 28 July as the pair sat within 50 pips of a multi-decade high. The squeeze catalyst then fired without warning. Pair-specific flow dynamics reinforce it: the uridashi/toshin channel that channels Japanese household savings into Australian-dollar paper is by construction a long AUD/JPY position held by price-insensitive holders who nonetheless reprice when the yen appreciates rapidly. Our expectation is that the 4 and 11 August COT reports show the combined yen short shrinking by 40,000 to 70,000 contracts, and that the covering is forced rather than discretionary.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Positioning mean-reverts within weeks and then rebuilds, so the strategic question is what the structural bilateral flow picture looks like once the squeeze completes, and here the answer is finely balanced but tilted against the pair. Supporting the pair: GPIF's May 2026 shift of seven percentage points out of JGBs into foreign equities is roughly USD 52bn of programmatic yen selling; Japanese residents bought JPY 1.09tn of foreign long-term bonds in a single early-July week; and the yen's share of allocated global reserves fell to 5.56% in Q1 2026. Opposing it: the ten major Japanese life insurers' FY2026 plans are explicitly defensive — none will increase unhedged foreign bonds, hedge ratios are rising, and the group plans to a term-end USD/JPY of 154, materially stronger than spot. Australian dollar paper is one of the classic destinations for exactly the unhedged foreign-bond allocation that all ten insurers have declined to increase, so the marginal structural bid under AUD/JPY from Japanese institutions has been withdrawn. On the Australian side, the superannuation system's roughly A$4.3 trillion creates a pro-cyclical equity-linked hedging channel that is currently AUD-supportive but reverses in exactly the drawdown that would also trigger Japanese repatriation — the two structural channels are positively correlated and both fire in the same direction against this pair.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the one factor that is unambiguously bullish AUD/JPY at the tactical horizon. Australia exported $46.7bn of goods to Japan in 2024 against $17.7bn of imports, a net goods surplus of $29.0bn on a 2.64:1 export-to-import ratio. The composition is overwhelmingly LNG, coal and iron ore — precisely the commodities whose prices have surged — so the bilateral trade relationship is a direct, mechanical income transfer from Japan to Australia that grows with the price level. Applying the framework's netting rules: oil up gives +AUD (mild) and --JPY (strong), net pair up; JKM LNG up at US$21.33-21.43/mmBtu (+78% y/y) gives --JPY and sometimes +AUD, net pair up strongly; Newcastle thermal coal at US$134.05/t (+16.4% y/y) is +AUD and -JPY; only iron ore at US$98.25/t (-0.9% y/y) is neutral-to-negative via weak Chinese demand. The magnitude differential is stark: Australia's terms-of-trade index sits at 96.4 and rising 1.1% quarter-on-quarter, while Japan's fell 5.0% in a single month to 83.95, 44% below its since-1960 average. Japan's June mineral fuel imports were JPY 2.10tn, up 41.9% year-on-year, producing a second consecutive monthly trade deficit at JPY 406.9bn against a JPY 120bn consensus.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.16 strategic weight this is the second-heaviest factor and it nets to genuinely zero, because price and stock point in opposite directions. The price channel remains pair-bullish: Australian LNG export earnings are forecast to rise from A$59bn to A$65bn on Middle East disruption. The stock and flow channel is decisively pair-bearish: Japan runs a current account surplus of 5.79% of GDP with a record JPY 34.52tn annual surplus, while Australia runs a deficit of 3.68% of GDP with a March-quarter shortfall of A$27,123m, the largest share of nominal GDP since June 2016, its first goods-and-services deficit since December 2017, and a A$23,656m net primary income drain. That is a 9.47 percentage point basic-balance differential in Japan's favour. Structurally, Australia's largest single export is contracting: iron ore earnings are forecast to fall from A$117bn to A$108bn against Chinese crude steel output down 3.0% in H1. The convexity is poor for the pair in both branches: if Hormuz escalates, Japan's terms of trade worsen (pair up) but the risk shock hits the highest-beta cross hardest (pair down); if Hormuz resolves, Japan's largest structural drag is removed (pair down) while Australia loses the export-price windfall (pair down). Resolution is unambiguously bearish and escalation is ambiguous — a concave payoff against extending any bullish read.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks are credible hawks that have delivered — the RBA 75bp across three 2026 meetings, the BoJ 100bp from negative rates with an 8-1 hold on 31 July in which Takata dissented for 1.25% — so standalone credibility scores are similar and would suggest a muted pair signal. The bilateral signal is not muted, for two reasons. First, the guidance-versus-pricing gap is asymmetric: the RBA's tightening bias is largely believed and largely priced, with little repricing room on the base leg; the BoJ's governor has said the Bank could speed up the pace of hikes, against September pricing of only 16-35% and 21bp cumulatively through December — a gap of 15-20 percentage points on a single meeting. Second, a third official actor has entered on the quote side with no counterpart on the base side. The RBA has explicitly stated the trade-weighted exchange rate is broadly consistent with its estimated long-run equilibrium; Japan's authorities have spent roughly JPY 20tn defending the yen in 2026 and have now recruited the US Treasury, with the intervention conducted under the September 2025 Joint Statement and plans to use the Fed's FIMA repo facility in future. Australia has no equivalent institutional bid for its currency and no equivalent institutional cap on it.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the factor weight nearly doubles to 0.12 and the bilateral asymmetry deepens. On the base side the RBA's credibility is a durable asset but a static one: already at 4.35%, ranked 1 of 11, with the market broadly aligned to its bias and the risk of losing rank 1 to Norges Bank inside the window. On the quote side credibility is dynamic: a board with a stated 2% neutral anchor, a hawkish dissenter already at 1.25%, three meetings and one quarterly Outlook Report inside the window, and an explicit US endorsement of normalisation. The Axios reading is that if the BoJ deals with currency weakness and inflation solely through rate hikes it accelerates the end of the carry trade, and a plausible interpretation of the US role is helping Japan act on yen weakness without creating Treasury-market stress — describing an institutional arrangement designed to make Japanese tightening cheaper to deliver. The strategic risk is Japanese domestic politics: Takaichi's LDP-Ishin coalition holds 352 of 465 lower-house seats on an expansionary platform, and a BoJ that pauses through October would leave the tactical squeeze as a completed event with nothing behind it. That is a real 30% scenario and it caps confidence at 60.

strategic.what_is_priced: The market prices a BoJ that hikes once more and stops, an RBA that holds, and an intervention regime that fades. We think the terminal-rate leg is the mispricing: OIS gives essentially no weight to a Japanese policy rate above 1.25% within twelve months, against a board framework implying 100bp and an allied Treasury publicly encouraging it.

factors.horizon_split: Both horizons are Bearish, with tactical confidence higher at 65 against 60 because the tactical case rests on dated, high-information publications inside the window plus an intervention regime that has just demonstrated itself. tactical.bilateral_analysis: Filtering both dossiers' calendars for bilateral impact produces an unusually front-loaded and quote-weighted cluster. Inside four weeks the events that matter, in order of impact, are the 10 August BoJ Summary of Opinions, the 11 August RBA decision plus August SoMP, the 19 August Japanese July trade balance, the 20 August Japanese national CPI, and the late-August MoF disclosure confirming intervention size — four of those five sit on the quote leg. The sequencing matters: the BoJ speaks on 10 August, setting the tone into an RBA decision on 11 August whose modal outcome is a hold. Layered on top is a genuinely undated, one-sided risk: Finance Minister Katayama confirmed the operation and warned the two countries could intervene together again if needed, framing Friday's action as countering excessive volatility and disorderly movements and saying it will not hesitate to conduct further joint intervention. There is no symmetric risk of official AUD selling. Bilateral political risk between Australia and Japan is negligible. The Hormuz situation remains the ambiguity.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the event distribution for this pair is genuinely two-sided. On one side, three BoJ meetings, a September Tankan, the 10 November US-China tariff truce expiry, mid-October China Q3 GDP, and a standing joint-intervention commitment are all pair-bearish. On the other, an RBA that could still hike, a possible Chinese stimulus package, and a Hormuz re-escalation that lifts Australian export prices while devastating Japanese terms of trade are pair-bullish. The Hormuz branch is uniquely ambiguous for this pair: a closure raising Brent above US$120 would drive Japan's terms of trade toward the 2022 record low (pair up) while triggering the global risk shock to which AUD/JPY has the highest beta in G10 (pair down). The China branch is one-sided negative: AUD/JPY is the most liquid China proxy among yen crosses, and China's Q2 GDP at 4.3% with a July PMI back in contraction is a deteriorating base-leg fundamental with no offset on the quote leg. Netting a one-sided negative China branch, a one-sided negative official-intervention branch and a genuinely two-sided energy branch, Neutral is the honest reading.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The fiscal and sovereign differential between these two issuers is the widest in any G10 pair and it is unambiguously pair-bullish. Australia holds AAA/Aaa/AAA ratings with a conventional, orderly ACGB curve carrying no visible credit premium at any tenor and commodity revenue realisations running 91-114% above Budget assumptions. Japan is rated A1/A+/A with debt revised up to 187.6% of GDP, a record FY2026 general-account budget of JPY 122.3tn, debt-service costs up 10.8% on an assumed 3.0% interest rate that is a 29-year high, and a 30-year JGB at 3.971% within 4bp of an all-time high. That is a four-to-five notch rating gap, the widest in the G10. The bilateral significance is the mechanism: Japan's fiscal risk premium is the specific channel by which higher Japanese yields have coincided with a weaker yen, exactly why the AU-JP ten-year spread compressed roughly 69bp over twelve months while AUD/JPY rose 10.14%. This factor is the reason the bearish thesis has failed for a year, and it remains live. Tactically there is no dated fiscal event on either side inside four weeks, so the factor is a background bullish drift rather than a catalyst.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the weight rises to 0.07 and the differential widens rather than narrows, the only factor scoring positive for the pair at both horizons. Japan is entering the first period in three decades in which rising rates cost the sovereign real money: refinancing a 187.6%-of-GDP stock at 30-year yields near 4% while the BoJ shrinks its holdings from roughly JPY 518tn toward a projected JPY 480tn by end-March 2027, with a sitting board member warning that halting the taper risks purchases being perceived as fiscal financing. Australia by contrast has commodity realisations 91-114% above Budget flowing into resource company tax receipts. The Australian 30-year at 5.49% yields 152bp more than the JGB 30-year at 3.971% despite a four-to-five notch stronger credit — the pair's yield advantage at the very long end has compressed sharply, entirely from Japan's credit premium widening rather than Australia's rate advantage narrowing. That is the fiscal-dominance channel in one number, and the specific mechanism by which the bearish thesis has failed for twelve months is alive, dated and outside our control.

The essential qualification is gap risk: the pair traversed 3.14 yen intraday on 30 July, so stop-loss discipline is unreliable, and the correct response is to cap risk with defined-outcome structures (put spreads financed by selling the 114.50-115.00 wing where the official cap now sits) rather than to rely on execution.

AUD/JPY is the most liquid non-USD yen cross and deepest pure risk-proxy cross in G10, but gap risk is materially elevated after the pair traversed 3.14 yen intraday on 30 July.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Global dollar conditions are abundant and uneventful, and for a cross they matter mainly as the oxygen supply of the carry trade. SOFR at 3.65% sits mid-range with no spread to IORB, EFFR at 3.63%, QT ended 1 December 2025 with the Fed's balance sheet at roughly USD 6,738bn and expanding, the 3M EUR/USD cross-currency basis is flat between -1bp and 0bp, and there is no swap-line usage. Cheap, plentiful dollars are pair-bullish because both legs settle through the dollar and because leverage is the input to carry. Against that sits a genuinely bilateral funding development: the Ministry of Finance announced plans to utilise the Fed's FIMA repo facility in future, which allows approved foreign monetary authorities to obtain short-term dollars by temporarily exchanging Treasury securities — giving Japanese authorities a way to borrow dollars against Treasuries rather than selling them outright. This removes the single largest historical constraint on sustained yen-buying intervention and converts the intervention threat from a one-shot to a repeatable, scalable instrument. That is directly pair-bearish. The two forces roughly offset at a 0.06 weight. The 3M AUD/JPY-relevant cross-currency basis is not publicly observable, a flagged gap.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.07 strategic weight the honest conclusion is that this factor generates no directional signal for the pair. The pair-bullish case is that abundant, cheap and stable dollars sustain leverage and therefore carry, with the Fed's balance sheet expanding for the first time since 2022. The pair-bearish cases are twofold: if the Fed drifts toward 4.00% as futures imply, the dollar moves to the 'US exceptionalism' leg of the smile, historically penalising AUD more than JPY; and the FIMA arrangement institutionalises the yen-support channel. There is a dated seasonal that cuts against the pair's bear case: the 31 December year-end funding turn reliably widens cross-currency basis and creates a temporary dollar bid, historically coinciding with a temporary rebuild of carry positions. The critical measurement gap is the 3M JPY/USD basis, which could not be sourced for a second consecutive cycle. Without it, asserting a direction would be a guess, and Neutral with confidence 50 is the accurate statement.

The score of -0.3481 therefore rests almost entirely on relative monetary trajectory: Policy & Rates at -0.1488 and Guidance & Credibility at -0.0720 together contribute 64% of the total, and both describe the same fact from different angles — Japan is the only G10 economy whose policy rate is unambiguously below its own central bank's neutral estimate, by 100bp, while Australia is at or above any published estimate and faces cuts in 2027. Where the dossiers interact, they reinforce: the AUD dossier is strategically Neutral (+0.018, conviction 2) and the JPY dossier is strategically Bullish JPY (+0.185, conviction 3), and both point to a lower pair. The bilateral factors that modify both standalone views are the official-sector regime change and the flow-channel correlation: analysts note that with US backing, interventions could prove more effective and more lasting than solo operations, the FIMA arrangement makes repetition sustainable, and all ten major Japanese life insurers have declined to increase unhedged foreign bond holdings, withdrawing precisely the structural bid that has historically underwritten Australian-dollar paper. What is priced versus what we expect is the sharpest divergence in this analysis: forwards embed only the mechanical 3.21% annualised carry roll-down to 109.10 at six months, published projections cluster between 115-117 as a bullish Q3 case and 107-108 as a bearish case and as high as 117.2-121.98 in statistical models for December 2026, while relative-REER fair value sits near 96. The path of least resistance is a stair-step erosion rather than a collapse, punctuated by carry-supported rallies that fail progressively lower, with the decisive break most likely around the 18 September or 30 October BoJ meetings. invalidators.mechanism: The pair's single largest bilateral asymmetry — an official-sector cap on the quote currency with no counterpart on the base currency — would be revealed as smaller and less durable than the April-May 2026 solo operation of JPY 11.73tn that failed. The pair's 15% premium to relative-REER fair value has persisted precisely because no credible cap existed; removing the cap restores the prior regime
invalidators.monitor_indicator: MoF monthly intervention disclosure and Treasury/MoF statements
invalidators.monitor_frequency: monthly for disclosure, continuous for statements

invalidators.condition: The combined CFTC leveraged-fund and asset-manager yen net short falls below 80,000 contracts while AUD/JPY remains above 110.00
invalidators.mechanism: That is the specific signature of a squeeze that has completed without producing a trend — the pair's downside fuel would be spent and price would not have moved, removing the 0.13-weighted Flows factor that contributes 24% of the tactical score. Because the pair's crowding is eight-to-one concentrated on the funding leg, a spent yen short leaves the pair with no positioning support for further downside at all
invalidators.monitor_indicator: CFTC Commitments of Traders, Japanese yen, leveraged funds plus asset managers

invalidators.condition: Iron ore breaks above US$115/t on a delivered Chinese LPR or RRR cut while VIX holds below 15 and copper makes new highs
invalidators.mechanism: This would simultaneously validate the base currency's terms-of-trade story, remove the China-deceleration argument that makes this the most exposed yen cross, and sustain the risk-on tape in which a 335bp carry gap dominates — the specific combination that would take the pair back above 114 and toward the 115-117 consensus zone
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Iron ore 62% Fe CFR China, PBoC LPR and RRR announcements, VIX
invalidators.monitor_frequency: daily for prices, monthly for the LPR

invalidators.condition: The 30-year JGB exceeds 4.25% while AUD/JPY simultaneously trades above 113.00
invalidators.mechanism: This is the definitive confirmation that Japanese yields are a fiscal credit risk premium rather than a policy premium — the exact configuration that produced roughly 69bp of AU-JP ten-year spread compression alongside a 10.14% rise in the pair over the last twelve months. In that regime, every basis point of Japanese yield increase weakens the yen rather than strengthening it, and the entire differential-compression thesis for this pair is void
invalidators.monitor_indicator: MoF constant-maturity 30-year JGB yield alongside AUD/JPY spot

invalidators.condition: Brent sustains above US$120 for two consecutive weeks on a renewed Hormuz closure while global equities hold within 5% of highs
invalidators.mechanism: The pair's terms-of-trade channel would dominate its risk channel — Japan's mineral fuel import bill, already up 41.9% year-on-year, would push its terms of trade toward the 69.80 record low while Australia's LNG and coal export earnings surged, and without an equity drawdown the pair's high beta would not offset it. This is the one geopolitical branch that is unambiguously pair-bullish
invalidators.monitor_indicator: Brent front-month, Hormuz transit counts, S&P 500 drawdown from high

signposts.confirms_if: narrows to 310bp or less on a delivered BoJ hike, or to 285bp on two
signposts.invalidates_if: widens to 360bp on an RBA hike with the BoJ holding through 30 October
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the pair's entire economic rationale. Unlike AUD/USD or USD/JPY, AUD/JPY has no second driver of comparable weight, so a 25bp move in the differential is a larger proportional shock to this pair's fair value than to any other G10 cross.
signposts.frequency: eight RBA meetings and eight BoJ meetings per year; OIS pricing daily

signposts.confirms_if: compresses below 280bp with the move led by the Japanese leg — specifically the 2Y JGB above 1.60%
signposts.invalidates_if: widens beyond 320bp, or compresses only because Australian yields fall while the 30-year JGB rises above 4.25%
signposts.bilateral_importance: The front end is the policy-sensitive part of the curve and therefore the clean test of whether the rate channel is functioning. This signpost matters more for AUD/JPY than for either currency alone because the pair's twelve-month history is a case study in the ten-year spread compressing while the pair rose — the composition of the compression, not its magnitude, is what determines direction here.

signposts.indicator: Combined CFTC yen net short versus AUD net long (pair-implied positioning)
signposts.current_level: JPY leveraged + asset managers -185,047 contracts (28 July) against AUD leveraged funds +24,788 (21 July) — an 8:1 notional concentration on the funding leg
signposts.confirms_if: the yen short falls by 40,000 or more over two reports while AUD/JPY trades below 109.50, showing covering is driving price
signposts.invalidates_if: the yen short falls below 80,000 contracts with the pair above 110.00, or rebuilds beyond 190,000
signposts.bilateral_importance: Netting the two legs is the only way to see that this pair's crowding is a funding-leg phenomenon. Neither dossier's standalone positioning read is actionable — AUD is mid-range at the 50th percentile — but the combination is beyond its historical extreme, and the pair can fall without any Australian liquidation at all.
signposts.frequency: weekly, Friday 15:30 ET, as at the prior Tuesday

signposts.indicator: AUD/JPY spot versus the 200-day and 100-day moving averages
signposts.confirms_if: a monthly close below 110.00, establishing a lower high at 114.92 and ending the uptrend from mid-2025
signposts.invalidates_if: three consecutive closes above 111.81 followed by a close above 113.08
signposts.bilateral_importance: AUD/JPY carries the deepest systematic participation of any non-USD yen cross, so its own moving-average configuration — not either currency's trade-weighted index — is the trigger for CTA and trend-following flow. A daily close above the 112.85-113.00 cluster is the level cited as necessary to ease the bearish bias, and until it is given the mechanical flow is one-directional.

signposts.current_level: US$21.33-21.43/mmBtu (+78% y/y), with Newcastle thermal coal at US$134.05/t
signposts.confirms_if: falls below US$14/mmBtu, signalling Hormuz normalisation, which removes Japan's largest structural terms-of-trade drag while stripping Australia of the export-price windfall
signposts.invalidates_if: sustains above US$25/mmBtu without a global equity drawdown, in which case the bilateral income transfer dominates
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the purest bilateral commodity variable in the pair, because Australia's $46.7bn of goods exports to Japan are dominated by exactly this commodity complex — a JKM move is simultaneously an Australian revenue line and a Japanese cost line, transmitting to AUD/JPY through both legs at once rather than through one. No other G10 pair has this structure.

signposts.indicator: Iron ore 62% Fe CFR China and the China NBS manufacturing PMI
signposts.current_level: iron ore US$98.25/t (-0.9% y/y, roughly -8% YTD); NBS manufacturing PMI 49.2 (July, back in contraction from 50.3)
signposts.confirms_if: iron ore below US$90/t with the PMI below 49.0, or China Q3 GDP below 4.0%
signposts.invalidates_if: iron ore above US$115/t on a delivered LPR or RRR cut with the PMI above 50.5
signposts.bilateral_importance: AUD/JPY is the most China-exposed yen cross with roughly 30% of Australian exports going to China and essentially no quote-leg offset, so Chinese data transmits asymmetrically — it damages the base currency's terms of trade and triggers the funding currency's safe-haven bid in the same move. For USD/JPY or EUR/JPY the same print is largely a risk-sentiment story; here it is a fundamental one.
signposts.frequency: daily for iron ore, monthly for the PMI

signposts.indicator: USD/JPY level as the intervention proxy
signposts.confirms_if: USD/JPY holds below 158.00, indicating the official coalition retains control and that AUD/JPY has no upside cover from a weakening yen complex
signposts.invalidates_if: USD/JPY reclaims 161.00 without a further official response, marking the joint operation as failed and reopening the yen-weakness regime across all crosses
signposts.bilateral_importance: AUD/JPY cannot rise durably while the yen is being defended, because the pair's rally has always been a yen-weakness story rather than an AUD-strength story — the pair is up 10.14% over twelve months while AUD/USD rose only 8.46%, so roughly a fifth of the move is pure yen. USD/JPY is the cleanest observable of the official reaction function, and it caps this cross mechanically.

signposts.indicator: VIX and US high-yield option-adjusted spread
signposts.current_level: VIX 17.09; ICE BofA US high-yield OAS 281-287bp, within roughly 46bp of the June 2007 all-time low
signposts.confirms_if: VIX sustains above 25 for five consecutive closes or high-yield OAS breaks 350bp
signposts.invalidates_if: VIX falls below 15 with high-yield OAS inside 270bp and realised pair volatility converging back below 6%
signposts.bilateral_importance: AUD/JPY is the framework's archetypal pure risk-proxy pair, so its beta to these two gauges is the highest in the G10 — a given move in high-yield spreads moves this pair roughly twice as far as it moves EUR/JPY and several times as far as it moves AUD/NZD. It is also the pair through which a carry unwind physically transmits, so these gauges are simultaneously a sentiment read and a positioning read here.

assumptions: Spot of 110.92087 (5 August close) is used as the source of truth even though the valuation date is 1 August, incorporating four sessions of post-intervention price action; the AUD dossier's own AUD/JPY mark of 111.52 dated 31 July differs by roughly 87 pips from the price series' 110.64897 for the same session, reflecting different closing conventions

The moving averages used (50d 112.61, 100d 113.08061, 200d 111.81008) are those supplied with the price data and treated as source of truth; third-party providers (FXStreet, FOREX.com) place these levels materially lower, likely because the supplied 390-observation series is calendar-based with weekend fills that flatten and bias the longer averages upward. The structural level 110.00 is convention-independent

AUD/JPY implied volatility is estimated, not observed, inferred from 20-day realised of 9.1%, the JPY dossier's pre-event 3M estimate of 9.5, and the observed spike in USD/JPY 1M implied to 12.5%; risk-reversal direction is sourced but magnitudes are not available

20-day realised volatility of 9.1% is computed from the 20 most recent weekday closes (8 July to 5 August) using standard deviation of daily log-approximate returns annualised at √252, excluding weekend fills present in the raw file

Forward points (-31/-92/-182/-356 pips at 1M/3M/6M/12M) are CIP-derived from the 4.35% RBA cash rate and 1.00% BoJ target rather than traded quotes; actual traded forwards will likely show a smaller discount and larger edge for a short position given narrower money-market spreads

Relative-REER fair-value estimates of 95.68 and 96.60 are taken directly from the two dossiers, constructed from BIS real broad effective exchange rates as deviations from each currency's own 30-month mean (January 2024-June 2026) and netted bilaterally — a relative misalignment measure, not an absolute PPP estimate, used as an ordinal attractor rather than a target

IMF DOTS bilateral trade data used as supplied without re-estimation; note the two-directional inconsistency between Australian-reported and Japanese-reported figures reflecting fob/cif and reporting-lag differences; data are for 2024 and predate the 2026 energy price surge, understating the current bilateral energy transfer

Five factor weights were adjusted, all within the ±0.05 limit; the Inflation & Growth Dynamics reduction (-0.02 tactical only) is disclosed as the weakest of the five — defensible but not compelling, and the analysis would reach near-identical scores at default weights

The strategic weighted score of -0.3481 maps to conviction 4 under the standard band structure but conviction 3 has been deliberately assigned as a judgement override, given the 182-pip carry cost (26% of base-case payoff) and the disconfirming evidence that the pair rose 10.14% over the last twelve months while the AU-JP ten-year spread compressed roughly 69bp

Public accounts of the 31 July intervention differ in framing (first joint intervention since 1998 for yen-buying specifically, since 2011 for any joint action, or since 15 years generically); the analysis uses 'first coordinated yen-buying intervention in nearly three decades' as the reconciled characterisation; the JPY dossier's estimated JPY 8.45tn size for the 30 July operation is an inference, not an official figure

Data gaps flagged and not estimated: 3M JPY/USD and AUD/USD cross-currency basis levels; AUD/JPY option barrier concentrations beyond round numbers; AUD/JPY 25-delta risk reversal magnitudes; confirmed size of the 31 July intervention (MoF disclosure due late August)
